title: Numerical Procedures: Cox-Ross-Rubinstein Binomial Trees, American Options, Control Variates, and Monte Carlo Simulation
prerequisites: Black-Scholes-Merton European option pricing and risk-neutral valuation
One-step and multi-step binomial tree fundamentals
Basic probability, normal distributions, and stochastic simulation
learningOutcomes: Construct Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial trees using up/down step factors $u$ and $d$ and risk-neutral probabilities $p$ ([fact-01]).
Value American options via backward induction by comparing immediate exercise value against discounted continuation value ([fact-02], [fact-03]).
Apply the control variate technique and escrow decomposition for discrete dividends to sharpen tree accuracy and preserve recombining efficiency ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
Execute risk-neutral Monte Carlo path simulation and calculate option price estimators and standard errors ([fact-06], [fact-07]).
Differentiate the comparative strengths of binomial trees (American exercise) versus Monte Carlo simulation (path-dependent exotic options) ([fact-08], [fact-09], [fact-10]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: American options require backward induction because the optimal early exercise decision depends on future node values, necessitating a recursive step from maturity back to time zero ([fact-02], [fact-08]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Direct subtraction causes tree branches to diverge into non-recombining node explosions ($2^N$), requiring Hull's escrow decomposition ($S^* = S - D \cdot e^{-r t_D}$) to preserve linear node growth ($N(N+1)/2$) ([fact-05]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Because standard error is inversely proportional to the square root of the path count ($SE \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$), quadrupling the number of paths ($4M$) is required to halve the standard error ([fact-07]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A 2-year American put option is valued on a CRR binomial tree with $S_0 = \$50, K = \$52, r = 5%, \sigma = 30\%$, and $\Delta t = 1$ year. Backward induction reveals optimal early exercise at node $(1,0)$ where stock price is $\$37.04$, yielding an immediate exercise profit of $\$14.96$ versus a continuation value of $\$12.36$. Separately, a Monte Carlo simulation generates terminal payoffs across $M$ paths.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) Why is early exercise optimal at node $(1,0)$ in this American put example? 2) How many simulated paths must be run to cut the Monte Carlo standard error in half?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial trees evaluate American options efficiently via backward induction, comparing immediate exercise against continuation values at every node ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Control variates and escrow decomposition eliminate discretization errors and prevent non-recombining node explosions when handling discrete dividends ([fact-04], [fact-05]).

Monte Carlo simulation excels at pricing complex path-dependent exotics, whereas binomial and trinomial trees remain the industry standard for American exercise features ([fact-06], [fact-08], [fact-09]).
